metadata.title: Occupational Health and Safety Platform Residuality Stress Test
metadata.description: Explore how a Belgian occupational health and safety software vendor (modeled, as an assumption, at about 70 people; Kitry does not publish headcount), serving 150+ organisations, 6,000+ active users and more than 4 million employee records with a modular HDS and ISO 27001 hosted SaaS in France, Belgium, Luxembourg and the Netherlands and backed by Vortex Capital Partners since March 2022, would need to change when France or Belgium rewrites surveillance periodicity and the DMST interoperability standard in the middle of the year, a data breach or an HDS/ISO 27001 non-conformity hits a platform holding millions of medical files, the telehealth, SMS or e-signature partner fails, reprices or is acquired, a large customer's HRIS migration floods the platform with bad worker data, an external prevention service or an HRIS vendor bundles occupational health software for free, a well-funded health-first competitor enters Belgium and the Netherlands, employee self-service climbs from half the workforce to ninety percent with mobile field reporting, AI-assisted drafting of fitness opinions and risk assessments raises liability and medical-council concerns, expansion to the Netherlands and Germany demands regulation content, languages and data residency the team cannot staff, or a buy-and-build acquisition brings a second product with its own medical data model and overlapping customers.
metadata.naiveArchitecture: An employer's occupational health service subscribes to the modules it needs. Workers, contracts, assignments, sites and workstations arrive from the HRIS in a nightly feed; each workstation carries an exposure profile; the surveillance engine derives the examination type and periodicity from the country's rules and the profile; convocations go out by SMS and e-mail through the partner gateways; the nurse runs the questionnaire, the connected devices and the intake; the physician records the consultation, issues the fitness opinion with restrictions, signs the certificate electronically and files everything in the occupational medical file; the prevention adviser keeps the risk assessment, the chemical inventory and the action plan; HR declares accidents on the national forms; employees and managers use their portals; the dashboards and annual reports summarise it all; and Kitry's own consultants configure, migrate, train and support every customer on shared or dedicated HDS hosting inside the EEA. The design assumes that a country's rules change between years rather than during them and are applied tenant by tenant by a consultant, that medical confidentiality is a role setting on one tenant database, that an SMS gateway, a video SDK and a signature API are wired into the bricks that use them, that the HRIS employee number identifies a worker and that a nightly feed is applied as it arrives, that the internal service is the buyer and the external prevention service and the HRIS are counterparts rather than competitors, that the product is what the last customer project produced, that self-service users are a minority who have a corporate e-mail address, that a physician is responsible for whatever text they sign, that a country is code plus a hiring plan, that the medical file follows one national profile in one region, and that there is one product.
metadata.residualArchitecture: The changed design separates country, rule set version and effective period, surveillance category, examination type and periodicity rule, DMST content standard and interoperability version, surveillance schedule version and delta, rule-version stamp on opinions, exports and reports, data class, access scope and purpose, consent and access grant, break-glass justification, tenant key, audit trail entry with record-level lineage, incident and affected-record set, control evidence and certification scope, integration capability, provider, contract and price schedule, adapter version, delivery attempt and fallback route, HRIS source, import batch, staging record, validation rule and anomaly threshold, worker identity with external key history and effective-dated assignment, recomputation run and rollback, capability, packaged offer, entitlement and pricing unit, counterpart service and exchange contract, medical file transfer record, product release train and version, user-experience metric per role, sector reference configuration, capacity model per tenant, asynchronous request and outcome, support tier and self-help route, media object with retention, AI capability, provider, model version and region, per-tenant AI policy, context scope, text provenance and human edit record, review and signature record, country package and version, locale, terminology set, hosting region and residency policy, certification scheme and control mapping, medical file profile, content author and partner certification, acquired product, shared identity and tenant registry, concept mapping, canonical record, migration state and lineage, capability parity and sunset plan. A fitness opinion knows which rule version, which device, which model and which person produced each part; a worker is an identity that survives an HRIS migration; a medical file can move between services, countries and products without being re-keyed; a customer can change hosting region, partner provider, AI policy, packaged offer or product on one day without changing systems.
metadata.note: The stressors start in the occupational health and safety trade: EU Framework Directive 89/391/EEC, the French law of 2 August 2021 strengthening prevention with its DMST decree of 15 November 2022 and the interoperability of occupational health information systems from 1 January 2024, the Belgian Code on well-being at work with its internal and external prevention services and Fedris, the HDS certification of health data hosts and ISO 27001, GDPR and medical secrecy, the EU AI Act's treatment of AI in health and employment, external prevention services and HRIS vendors bundling tooling, health-first competitors funded at scale, the Dutch Arbowet and NEN 7510 and the German ArbMedVV, and the Vortex thesis of commercial scaling, international rollout and selective acquisitions. They are not forecasts and assign no likelihood; each asks what must remain after the vendor is pushed into a different attractor. The regulatory-rewrite, security and HRIS-migration scenarios are recorded as residues the platform already carries; the self-service wave is the loop that tests whether those residues hold without new structure.

source.title: Residues: Time, Change, and Uncertainty in Software Architecture
source.author: Barry M. O'Reilly

stressors.name: France or Belgium rewrites surveillance periodicity and the DMST interoperability standard in the middle of the year
stressors.detection: Journal officiel and Moniteur belge publications; decrees under the French law of 2 August 2021 such as decree 2022-1434 on the content of the DMST and the interoperability deadline for occupational health information systems; new versions of the Agence du Numérique en Santé interoperability framework and the DMST content standard; Belgian changes to the Code on well-being at work that move periodic health assessments between annual, biennial and risk-based intervals per surveillance category; the number of workers whose next examination date moves under the new rule; convocations already sent for dates that the new rule no longer requires; physicians asking which periodicity applies to a night worker with a chemical exposure; rejected DMST exports; the regulatory-content team's watch list of consultations and draft decrees; and consultant hours spent updating tenants one by one.
stressors.attractor: In June, France changes the examination types and intervals for several special surveillance categories and publishes a new DMST content and interoperability version with a deadline in January, while Belgium moves one category from annual to biennial assessment. Across 150+ organisations and more than 4 million employee records, every surveillance schedule computed under the old rule must be recomputed, convocations already sent must be reconciled, capacity plans per physician change, the DMST export must render the new version while files transferred from other services stay readable in the old one, and the annual activity report must state which rule applied to which period. In the naive design periodicity is a parameter per exposure category configured per tenant by a consultant, a schedule does not know which rule version produced it, the DMST export is compiled to one standard version, the fitness opinion template embeds the examination type as text, and Kitry's consultants apply the change to 150 tenants one at a time while the physicians keep a spreadsheet of who is overdue under the new rule.
stressors.businessReaction: Model country regulation as versioned rule sets with effective periods; express examination types, periodicity, special surveillance categories, DMST content and interoperability versions and report requirements as machine-readable rules that the surveillance engine, scheduling, consultation templates, medical file export and annual reports consume; recompute schedules across all tenants with a delta report of workers newly due, no longer due or rescheduled; reconcile sent convocations against the delta; stamp every schedule, opinion, export and report with the rule version in force; make the DMST export render any supported standard version and read earlier ones; publish regulatory alerts in the dashboard; run the regulatory-content team's work as a change workflow from detection to release with a lead-time target; and include regulatory releases in the SaaS subscription rather than as consultant projects.
stressors.residue: Separate country, rule set version and effective period, surveillance category, examination type and periodicity rule, DMST content standard and interoperability version, surveillance schedule version and delta, convocation reconciliation, rule-version stamp on opinions, exports and reports, regulatory alert and change. Compliance becomes a property computed per worker from the rule in force rather than a parameter a consultant typed into a tenant.

impacts.effect: Occupational physicians see a regulatory change applied to every worker's next examination the day it is released, not after a project.

Every required examination is derived from the rule set with an effective period, so current and prior obligations stay correct at the same time.

The annual activity report states which rule version applied to which period.
A workforce data change triggers surveillance under the rule in force on that date, not the rule configured at go-live.
A regulatory release reaches all tenants at once with a change log instead of 150 configuration visits.
Medical surveillance compliance rate holds through a mid-year change because the change is a versioned rule release, not a rewrite.
Workforce surveillance coverage rate is reported per rule version so a periodicity change does not appear as a coverage collapse.

Reports compliance and activity per rule version and effective period.
Delivers regulatory releases as part of the subscription with a lead-time target.
Re-runs the schedule on a rule change and reconciles convocations already sent against the delta.
Exports and imports the DMST in any supported standard version.
Treats a regulatory release as a change workflow from detection to all-tenant release.
Versions country rule sets with effective periods and exposes categories, examination types, periodicity and DMST versions as rules.
Computes schedules from the rule version in force and produces the delta against the earlier schedule version.
Reconciles sent convocations against the recomputed schedule and reschedules by exception.
Sends rescheduling notices from the delta rather than from a manual list.

Reports activity and compliance per rule version and period.

Owns the rule model and the change workflow with workforce and surveillance, medical records and analytics.

stressors.name: A data breach or an HDS/ISO 27001 non-conformity hits a platform holding millions of occupational medical files
stressors.detection: Findings from HDS certification audits under article L.1111-8 of the French Public Health Code and from ISO 27001 surveillance audits; penetration test results on the employee portal and the consultant back office; access to medical files by non-medical roles or from outside the EEA in the audit trail; credential stuffing against portal accounts; a lost consultant laptop; the 72-hour breach notification duty to the CNIL or the Belgian Data Protection Authority; CNIL guidance on occupational health data; security questionnaires from customers of SNCF, Engie or BNP scale; works council questions about who can read what; media reports of health-data breaches at French hospitals; and the contractual clause that suspends use of the platform if certification lapses.
stressors.attractor: An attacker enters through a compromised consultant account with cross-tenant support access and exfiltrates medical files from a shared hosting environment, or the HDS audit records a major non-conformity on backup encryption and access from outside the EEA. Kitry must notify 150+ organisations and their works councils within days, determine which files were read, prove which roles accessed which records, contain the incident without stopping the 149 unaffected customers, and face a suspended certification that contractually stops customers from using the platform. In the naive design confidentiality is a role setting, a medical file is a set of rows in the tenant database, the audit trail is log lines, incident scope is reconstructed from logs by hand, one shared environment means one incident touches every customer, consultant superuser access is a support convenience, and certification is a document rather than a property of the running system.
stressors.businessReaction: Separate data class (medical secrecy, administrative, safety) from role; model access scope and purpose per read with consent and access grants and a break-glass path with justification and review; encrypt per tenant with tenant-held keys; make the audit trail record-level so the incident's affected-record set is computed rather than reconstructed; give consultants time-bound, approved, logged access per tenant instead of standing superuser rights; contain at tenant level so shared hosting can isolate one customer; map running controls continuously to the HDS and ISO 27001 control sets and keep the evidence; prepare breach communication packs for customers, works councils and authorities; and add security reviews and evidence to the account management cadence.
stressors.residue: Separate data class, access scope and purpose, consent and access grant, break-glass justification, tenant key, audit trail entry with record-level lineage, incident and affected-record set, control evidence and certification scope, containment action. Confidentiality becomes a computed property of each read rather than a role setting on a database.

stressors.name: The telehealth, SMS or e-signature partner fails, reprices or is acquired
stressors.detection: Status pages and incident notices from Vonage, Cegedim and Goodflag; API deprecation notices after an acquisition such as Ericsson's of Vonage; per-message SMS price changes and delivery rates per country operator; teleconsultation join failures reported by physicians on consultation day; qualified certificate chain changes under eIDAS that invalidate a signature workflow; no-show rates rising when reminders stop; customer procurement asking for an alternative provider or for a provider already under group contract; questions about where video streams and message logs are stored; and the cost of partner services inside the subscription margin.
stressors.attractor: The SMS provider triples its price per message in France, the telehealth vendor announces the end of the video API twelve months after being acquired, and the e-signature provider changes its certificate chain. Convocation reminders for millions of workers stop or become unaffordable, teleconsultations fail on the day, fitness certificates cannot be signed, and no-shows climb across the customer base. In the naive design each partner is wired into the brick that uses it: the scheduler calls the SMS API directly, the consultation workspace embeds one video SDK, the document brick calls one signature API, credentials live per tenant, the partner's cost is buried in the subscription price, and switching means a release and a migration for every tenant.
stressors.businessReaction: Model an integration capability (messaging, video consultation, signature, device capture) separately from the provider, the provider contract and price schedule, the region and the per-tenant channel policy; build adapters against a conformance suite; route each request through a fallback (e-mail and portal push when SMS fails, telephone consultation when video fails, a deferred signing queue when the certificate chain breaks); track every delivery attempt and session outcome; show provider health and cost per message per tenant in the operations dashboard; keep a second provider under contract per capability; and negotiate partner terms at the level of the Vortex portfolio rather than per vendor.
stressors.residue: Separate integration capability, provider, provider contract and price schedule, adapter version, credential set, delivery attempt and outcome, fallback route, provider health signal, per-tenant channel policy. A reminder, a video session or a signature becomes a capability request routed to whichever provider is available and allowed.

impacts.effect: Nurses run the consultation day whether the reminders went by SMS, e-mail or portal push.
Employees join a teleconsultation by whichever channel works and sign documents when the certificate chain is back.
A partner outage degrades to a fallback channel rather than cancelling the day.
Fitness opinions are issued on time and signed through a deferred queue if the signature provider fails.
Appointment reminders reach the worker through the tenant's policy of channels.
Capacity planning includes provider health and no-show rates per channel.

Examinations completed per nurse day hold because sessions and reminders route around a failed provider.
Becomes a video capability with provider adapters and a telephone fallback instead of one vendor's SDK.
Carries provider contracts, adapters, conformance tests and health per capability.
Requests messaging, video and signature as capabilities with per-tenant channel policy.
Falls back from video to telephone and from immediate to deferred signing.
Sends reminders through a routed channel policy and records every delivery attempt.
Manages provider contracts, adapters and second sources per capability.
Separates capability from provider, versions adapters and keeps a second provider per capability.
Routes reminders by tenant channel policy with fallback and delivery outcomes.
Runs on any conformant video adapter and degrades to telephone consultation.

stressors.name: A large customer's HRIS migration floods the platform with bad worker data
stressors.detection: A customer announces a move to SAP SuccessFactors, Workday or a new payroll provider; import batch rejection rates and duplicate worker identifiers; a nightly feed in which tens of thousands of workers appear as leavers and joiners at once; workstation and cost centre codes that no longer match the site structure; a surge of surveillance schedules newly due or cancelled; physicians finding files attached to the wrong worker; HR tickets about missing employees; convocations sent to terminated workers; and consultant hours spent on reconciliation instead of go-lives.
stressors.attractor: A rail or utility group with 100,000 workers re-keys every employee number in its new HRIS, reshapes the organisation and sends a full load in which 40,000 workers leave and 40,000 join on the same night. The nightly import applies it: surveillance schedules are cancelled and recreated, convocations for the cancelled ones are withdrawn by SMS, new workers have no exposure profile and no history, and medical files keyed on the old employee number are orphaned. In the naive design the feed is applied directly to the worker registry, a worker is identified by the HRIS employee number, an assignment change immediately recomputes surveillance and notifies, medical files are linked by that key, and the consultants restore from a backup and re-run a week of work by hand.
stressors.businessReaction: Separate the import batch from the applied change: stage every batch, validate it against a rule set with anomaly thresholds that halt application (for example more than five percent leavers in one night), match identities on a stable internal worker id with a history of external keys, give HR and consultants a reconciliation workbench, apply assignments with effective dates, defer schedule recomputation behind a delta preview, bind medical files to the internal identity and never to the HRIS key, allow replay and rollback of a batch, ship the HRIS migration runbook as a product feature, and report a data quality score per tenant.
stressors.residue: Separate HRIS source, import batch, staging record, validation rule and anomaly threshold, identity match and external key history, applied change with effective date, schedule recomputation run and delta, batch rollback, data quality score. A worker is an identity with a history of external keys, not a row from last night's file.

Work accident declaration on-time rate is not disrupted because declarations bind to the stable worker identity.

stressors.name: An external prevention service or an HRIS vendor bundles occupational health software for free
stressors.detection: IDEWE, Belgium's largest external prevention service with 35,000 employers and about 880,000 employees, and Mensura with 50,000+ customers offering employer portals with convocations, fitness attestations and risk assessment tooling inside the statutory contribution; more than 99.5 percent of Belgian companies using an external service; HRIS and payroll vendors such as SAP SuccessFactors, Workday, Cegid or SD Worx listing a health and safety or absence module; renewal negotiations that cite an included alternative; tenders that require integration with the external service's portal; customers with mixed internal and external services; and win-loss notes where price per user was the reason.
stressors.attractor: A large Belgian employer's external prevention service ships a portal that covers convocations, fitness attestations and a basic risk assessment, bundled with the mandatory contribution, while its HRIS vendor adds an OHS module to the suite. Procurement asks why they pay for a modular platform whose basics are now included twice. In the naive design Kitry sells an all-in-one modular platform licensed per module (Kitry does not publish pricing; the modeled assumption), assumes the internal service is the buyer, treats the external service as a counterpart to exchange data with and the HRIS as a data source, cannot run only the parts the bundles do not cover, and proves its value in annual reports rather than in measured outcomes.
stressors.businessReaction: Unbundle the platform into capabilities that can run alongside an external service's portal and an HRIS module: the internal service's system of record for large employers, exchange of fitness attestations and convocation status with external services, medical file transfer between services as a product, and the specialist depth the bundles lack (chemicals and exposures, ISO 45001, accidents and occupational diseases, collective health monitoring, multi-country); price per worker covered rather than per module; measure and publish value per customer (surveillance compliance, declaration timeliness, action closure); partner with external services through dedicated or white-label hosting; list in HRIS marketplaces; and package sector pre-configurations.
stressors.residue: Separate capability, packaged offer, entitlement, pricing unit, counterpart service and exchange contract, medical file transfer record, value metric per tenant. The platform becomes a set of capabilities entitled per employer and interoperable with the services that surround it.

stressors.name: A well-funded health-first competitor enters Belgium and the Netherlands
stressors.detection: Padoa's EUR 80 million raise in February 2022 with Five Arrows Growth Capital and its share of French inter-company services; job postings in Brussels and Amsterdam and Dutch-language product pages; Val Solutions' uEgar covering 12 million workers and 12,000 health professionals in France; physicians praising a physician-designed consultation interface in tender evaluations; per-worker pricing in competing bids; lost tenders in the public sector; physicians moving between services and carrying their preferences; and references shifting from Kitry to the entrant.
stressors.attractor: The entrant opens a Benelux office, brings a modern physician-first consultation experience, a mobile employee app, transparent pricing per worker and a marketing budget, wins a marquee Belgian public-sector tender and starts to earn the loyalty of the physicians who evaluate Kitry's renewals. In the naive design Kitry's differentiation is 35 years of regulatory know-how, blue-chip references and services; the interface evolves through customer configuration; releases follow projects; product decisions come from consultants; the user experience is not measured; and retention rests on the cost of migrating decades of medical files.
stressors.businessReaction: Run a product-led roadmap on a standard release train; measure the physician and nurse experience (documentation time, clicks per consultation, questionnaire completion) per role and per release; build a design system across modules; make the employee and manager portals mobile-first; keep tender-ready reference configurations per sector; publish transparent per-worker pricing and compliance outcomes; use Vortex-backed sales and marketing capacity; and keep the depth the entrant lacks (chemicals, accidents and occupational diseases, ISO 45001, multi-country content) as the moat.
stressors.residue: Separate product release train and version, user-experience metric per role, design system component, sector reference configuration, pricing plan and entitlement, competitor watch and win-loss record. The product becomes something Kitry ships on its own cadence rather than the outcome of the last project.

stressors.name: Employee self-service climbs from half the workforce to ninety percent and mobile field reporting changes load and support patterns
stressors.detection: Self-service rates above fifty percent in French, Belgian and Luxembourg customers; a customer with 100,000 workers mandating portal-only convocations with single sign-on; login peaks minutes after each convocation batch; hazardous situation reports with photos arriving from phones at ten times the earlier rate; password resets and cannot-log-in tickets outnumbering consultant tickets; portal sessions from shift workers at night; storage growth from photos; works council questions about tracking portal use; and nurses receiving rescheduling requests all day.
stressors.attractor: A group of 100,000 workers switches convocations to portal-only with SSO and a site rollout turns every worker into a reporter of hazardous situations from the phone. Login peaks follow every convocation batch, rescheduling requests flood the nurses, hazard reports arrive at ten times the rate with photos, and support shifts from 6,000 professionals to hundreds of thousands of occasional users. The naive design sized the portal for a minority, assumed a worker without a corporate e-mail address is an exception, ran notifications and slot booking synchronously, stored photos in the database, and routed end-user support to the same desk that serves consultants and physicians.
stressors.businessReaction: Loop test rather than new design: access scope, consent and tenant isolation already exist from the security residue, and worker identity with external key history already exists from the HRIS residue, so a mandated portal rollout does not need a new identity or confidentiality model. Add capacity as a property per tenant: asynchronous notification and slot booking with queuing at batch time, passwordless and one-time-code options for workers without corporate e-mail, a self-help and tenant-administrator support tier, a media store for photos with retention, triage of hazard reports by site and severity, portal adoption analytics per customer, and an adoption playbook in the implementation method.
stressors.residue: Reuses access scope, consent and access grant, tenant isolation, worker identity and external key history; adds capacity model per tenant, asynchronous request and outcome, support tier and self-help route, media object with retention, report triage rule, adoption metric. The residues from the security and HRIS stressors hold; the portal becomes a capacity to plan rather than a feature to switch on.

stressors.name: AI-assisted drafting of fitness opinions and risk assessments raises liability and medical-council concerns
stressors.detection: Customer requests to summarise consultation notes and pre-fill the DUERP or the global prevention plan; the EU AI Act treating AI used in health and in employment decisions as high-risk with human oversight, logging and risk management duties; positions of the French Ordre des médecins and the Belgian Orde der artsen on AI and the physician's independent judgement; CNIL guidance on AI and health data; HDS constraints on processing outside the EEA; works council questions; physicians refusing to sign drafted text; a disputed fitness opinion in a labour court where the draft was generated; and competitors advertising AI features.
stressors.attractor: Kitry ships assisted drafting of fitness opinions and risk assessments. A physician signs a drafted opinion that omits a restriction; the worker is injured; the labour court asks who wrote the text and what the physician changed; the medical council asks whether independent judgement was exercised; the works council asks whether health data left the EEA; and the AI Act's high-risk obligations apply to the vendor and the employer. In the naive design AI is a button in the consultation workspace that calls one provider, drafted text is inserted without provenance, the model sees the whole file, there is no per-tenant policy, no record of what the human changed, and the physician is assumed responsible for whatever they signed.
stressors.businessReaction: Record text provenance per section of an opinion or assessment (drafted by which model version, edited how by which person, signed when); model AI capability, provider, model version and region separately with a per-tenant and per-role AI policy that can be switched off on one day; run models inside the EEA under HDS with minimum-necessary context; enforce a human-oversight workflow with mandatory review before signature; keep the oversight log and a documented risk management system as the AI Act requires; engage the medical councils on the physician's role; set contractual responsibility per document section; and prepare an evidence pack for disputes.
stressors.residue: Separate AI capability, provider, model version and region, per-tenant AI policy, context scope, draft, text provenance and human edit record, review and signature record, oversight log, dispute evidence pack. An opinion knows which words came from the model, which from the physician and which rule version applied.

stressors.name: Expansion to the Netherlands and Germany demands regulation content, languages and data residency that a 70-person team cannot staff
stressors.detection: The Vortex thesis of international rollout; existing Dutch and German subsidiaries of French and Belgian customers; the Dutch Arbowet and Arbobesluit, certified arbodiensten, the bedrijfsarts role and PMO and PAGO examinations; NEN 7510 asked for where HDS is unknown; the German ArbMedVV, DGUV rules and the Betriebsarzt; German-language requirements; tender questions on data residency; the difficulty of hiring occupational health content specialists for new countries; translation backlogs; and consultant bandwidth already consumed by French and Belgian go-lives.
stressors.attractor: A Dutch multinational customer wants the Netherlands as a full market and its German plants on the same platform. In the naive design regulation content lives as French, Belgian and Luxembourg configuration authored by a small team, the interface exists in three languages, hosting is one region under HDS, the medical file assumes the DMST profile, national forms are built per country, delivery depends on Kitry's own consultants, and partnering with arbodiensten or German Betriebsärzte is not modeled. Each country becomes a hiring plan the company cannot execute.
stressors.businessReaction: Make a country a first-class content package (rules, forms, reports, national connectors, terminology) with a version and a certified author model that includes partners; separate locale from country; add a residency policy per tenant and region; map the HDS control set to NEN 7510 and ISO 27001 so certification is a mapping, not a second programme; generalise the medical file so the DMST is one profile; deliver through local partners; prioritise the Netherlands before Germany; and consider acquiring local content vendors.
stressors.residue: Separate country package and version, locale, terminology set, hosting region and residency policy, certification scheme and control mapping, medical file profile, content author and partner certification, delivery partner. A country becomes content and policy rather than code and a hiring plan.

stressors.name: A Vortex buy-and-build acquisition brings a second product with its own medical data model and overlapping customers
stressors.detection: The Vortex thesis of selective acquisitions adding geography or adjacent capability; target lists of Dutch arbodienst software, French safety and chemicals vendors and DUERP tools; a letter of intent; customer overlap analysis; two support desks, two identity systems, two hosting certifications and two release trains; medical record models that differ (visit-centric against file-centric, different fitness opinion semantics); customers asking which product is the roadmap; and physicians who use both products.
stressors.attractor: Kitry acquires a Dutch occupational health SaaS with two hundred customers, some of them shared. Both products hold workers, medical files and fitness opinions with different semantics; both promised customers a merged product; the medical file transfer that Kitry built between services assumes Kitry is the source. In the naive design there is one product, one tenant model and one data model, migration is a consultant project per customer, identity, support and certification exist per product, and the roadmap cannot say when the two become one.
stressors.businessReaction: Build a shared identity and customer-tenant registry across products; define a concept mapping and canonical record for worker, workstation, exposure, visit, opinion and file; make medical file migration a product capability with lineage in both directions; keep a capability parity matrix and a sunset plan; unify support and account management; share regulatory content and hosting certification; publish one commercial catalogue; and track migration state per customer so the switch happens on one day.
stressors.residue: Separate product, shared identity and tenant registry, concept mapping, canonical record, migration state and lineage, capability parity, sunset plan, consolidated contract and entitlement. A customer moves between products without re-keying medical files.
